\chapter{Grandparents, and the Married Pair}
\label{ch:ml-grandparents}
\hlchaptermodality{45}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name four more family and people words in this language.}

Complete ML-C45-wife and say all four words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[muttacchan]{\ml{മുത്തച്ഛൻ} (muttacchan) — grandfather}

\label{lesson:ML-C45-grandfather}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{eḻutū} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മുത്തച്ഛൻ}}
\textbf{\ml{മുത്തച്ഛൻ}} (\emph{muttacchan}) — \textquotedblleft{}grandfather\textquotedblright{}.

Two pieces, both audible: \emph{mutta-}, 'elder, senior', and \emph{acchan}, the 'father' from the family lesson. Literally, an elder father. Where Sanskrit would reach for a compound of its own, Malayalam assembles this one out of words the learner already owns.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of four family words. Three follow, and each reuses the ones before.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{muttacchan}
  \item it once more, slowly, hearing the two halves
  \item it after \emph{eḻutū}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{മുത്തച്ഛൻ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}grandfather\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[muttaśśi]{\ml{മുത്തശ്ശി} (muttaśśi) — grandmother}

\label{lesson:ML-C45-grandmother}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{muttacchan} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മുത്തശ്ശി}}
\textbf{\ml{മുത്തശ്ശി}} (\emph{muttaśśi}) — \textquotedblleft{}grandmother\textquotedblright{}.

The same \emph{mutta-} opens it, so half the word is already yours. The second half is not as transparent as the grandfather word's: \emph{-aśśi} is an old term of address for an elder woman rather than the everyday \emph{amma} you already know, and dictionaries stop short of a confident breakdown. Better to flag that than to pretend the two halves match.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of four, and one honest gap in the analysis.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{muttaśśi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{muttacchan}, and name the half they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{മുത്തശ്ശി} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}grandmother\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bharttāvŭ]{\ml{ഭർത്താവ്} (bharttāvŭ) — husband}

\label{lesson:ML-C45-husband}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{muttaśśi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ഭർത്താവ്}}
\textbf{\ml{ഭർത്താവ്}} (\emph{bharttāvŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}husband\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{bhartṛ} with a Malayalam ending, \emph{-āvŭ}, fitted onto it. Inside sits the root \emph{bhṛ}, 'to bear, to carry, to support', so the word says 'the one who supports'. The root is old enough to have relatives well outside India: Latin \emph{fero}, 'I carry', and English \emph{bear} both continue it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three of four. The last word grows from the same root.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bharttāvŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{muttaśśi}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{ഭർത്താവ്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}husband\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhārya]{\ml{ഭാര്യ} (bhārya) — wife}

\label{lesson:ML-C45-wife}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bharttāvŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{ഭാര്യ}}
\textbf{\ml{ഭാര്യ}} (\emph{bhārya}) — \textquotedblleft{}wife\textquotedblright{}.

The same root \emph{bhṛ} as the last word, ending differently: 'she who is to be supported'. Telugu borrowed the identical pair from Sanskrit, so \emph{bharta} and \emph{bhārya} there are these two words again, wearing local endings. What the pair records is Sanskrit's older picture of a household, not a modern one — worth saying out loud rather than smoothing over.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
That closes the run: grandfather, grandmother, husband, wife.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bhārya}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{bharttāvŭ}, and name the root they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{ഭാര്യ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}wife\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
